content.title: THE ULTIMATE VEGAN NOT VEGAN GUIDEBOOK
content.subtitle:
HOW TO MAKE THE TRANSITION TO A PLANT-BASED LIFESTYLE WITHOUT THE EMOTIONAL WHIPLASH
BY COSMIC KITTY IN SPACE/ANA NOT ANA

content.heading: FORWARD
paragraphs: TO EVERY ANIMAL THAT WAS KILLED AGAINST THEIR WILL, ACTIVISTS ARRESTED FOR SAVING THEM, AND VEGANS ALL AROUND THE WORLD WHO FIGHT FOR THE RIGHTS OF ANIMALS EVERY SINGLE DAY, THIS IS FOR YOU.

content.heading: FIRSTLY, CONGRATU-FUCKING-LATIONS
paragraphs: This required you to face some things in your life that probably weren't easy. Whatever the reason that made you decide to go plant-based (see how I didnt say “vegan”; I did this for a reason)*, you had to confront certain realities either about the wellbeing of the animals, the health of the planet, your levels of empathy, our current food industry, and honestly, how many lies you’ve been told (and maybe had to tell yourself to maintain the illusion of your decision until now)

content.heading: SECONDLY, CONGRATU-FUCKING-LATIONS AGAIN.
paragraphs: The rug of dietary deceit slapped me in the face once I *really saw* what was happening to the animals in the slaughterhouses and factory farms. Unfortunately, that was only the beginning. What was truly horrific was how indifferent people around me seemed to be when I shared this information with them.

I made this guide so you don’t feel alone when you make this transition. You will lose friends, and maybe even some family. The truth is unsettling, and it can make you feel like you’re crazy when you’re the only one at the dinner saying “no thank you” to the dead carcass everyone is celebrating over.

My whole life changed when I woke up to the reality of the factory farm and slaughterhouse industry. My initial research explored solutions to end plastic production at its root while promoting alternative organic-based products (like mycelium and seaweed packaging). However, as I looked into plastic's destructive nature, I started noticing other harmful industries. I started mapping similarities between the energetic signature of *how* plastic was made (violent extraction through fracking and the invasion of nature) and the energetic signature of factory farms, the treatment of the homeless, how poverty is subtly passed on and structurally instituted, the obsession with violence and domination through the military-industrial complex, and lastly, the normalization of modern-day slavery through covert and overt intercontinental operations.
IMAGE CREATED BY @COSMICKITTYINSPACE

content.text: What happens to the animals eventually happens to man.

paragraphs: There is no point in protesting on the streets to end genocide when you go back and consume the body of an animal that went through their own genocide. No point in standing by Black lives when you participate in the same currency that created slavery in the same place.
As I said above, this was not an easy truth to contend with.

The more research I did, the more I started to hate humanity and everyone who still decided to be blind to the suffering of these animals by consuming their dead bodies. I found it increasingly more difficult to be friends with people who had been in my life for over 17 years. I said no to weddings and birthdays, dinner parties, holiday gatherings; anything where non-vegan communal food was to be shared.

I saw the truth. Why couldn’t they? Were my friends and family really psychopaths? Why don’t they care about the animals? I thought they loved animals. Why are they making me feel bad about this? Why are they making fun of me? I thought they loved me?...

These were some thoughts and feelings that I started to have as I made my transition to a vegan diet. I suddenly found myself alone in parking lots waiting for my family to finish dinner when we ate out.

I WAS SUDDENLY INCREDIBLY REPULSED BY ANYONE EATING MEAT AND DID NOT UNDERSTAND HOW I HAD EATEN MEAT FOR ALL THOSE YEARS. I SHOULD ALSO MENTION THAT I HAD STOPPED DRINKING ALCOHOL AROUND THE SAME TIME, WHICH ACCELERATED THE PATH TOWARD CLARITY AND ISOLATION.
WHEN WE START TO UNTANGLE THE WEBS OF TORTURE AND DESTRUCTION WITHIN OUR LIVES, WE INEVITABLY START TO MAKE CLEANER PATHS THAT GIVE US A SENSE OF RENEWAL.

I’VE NOT HAD ANY DEAD MEAT IN MY BODY FOR OVER 7 YEARS. MY LIFE HAS COMPLETELY CHANGED. MY INNER WORLD HAS COMPLETELY SHIFTED, AND THE DECISIONS THAT I MAKE IN MY LIFE NOW ARE GUIDED BY A MUCH DEEPER SENSE OF PURPOSE AND UNDERSTANDING.
I HOPE YOU FIND WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR IN THIS GUIDE AND THAT YOU SHARE IT WITH ANYONE WHO HAS EXPRESSED ANY INTEREST IN CHANGING TO A PLANT-BASED DIET.

content.heading: THIRDLY, YOU ARE NOT ALONE.
paragraphs: There are countless Facebook groups, Instagram pages, online or in-person support groups, communities, chats, and forums that offer advice, recipes, and support. Even though we are the minority (only 1% of the world is vegan/plant-based), we are certainly not alone or unsupported. I highly recommend finding a community of people who have made this switch so you don’t feel overwhelmed with this change. (Or Join our Discord)

The onslaught of truth can leave you emotionally distraught. Do not let yourself wrestle with this alone. I was 28 when I realized the truth behind factory farms and my role in meat and dairy consumption. At that point, I had over 10,15, 20 + years of being a complicit animal abuser.
Forgive yourself.

content.text:
FACTORY FARMING HAS NORMALIZED TORTURE + MURDER FOR CORPORATE + MILITARY GAIN

TRAPPING US INTO AN ENERGETIC WEB OF CHAOS, ANXIETY, DEPRESSION, AND PAIN.

paragraphs: When we consume products from a slaughterhouse, aka a torture chamber, we inevitably reinforce the very same energetic ties that many of us want to break free from in our daily lives. Instead of protesting on the streets every few months, we can protest every day with the dietary choices that we make. When we redirect our attention and purchasing power to a practice that carries harmonic resonance with peace, non-violence, and regeneration, we strengthen a web that reinforces an existence founded upon these principles.

content.heading: PURCHASING POWER AND THE ECONOMICS BEHIND THE SHIFT

paragraphs: When we consume ANYTHING from the egg, meat, and dairy industries, we inevitably give this industry our POWER. This power gets compounded over time. Ultimately, we have to ask ourselves: which structures do we want to weaken, and which energetic currencies do we want to strengthen? Demand and Supply mechanisms work organically. We know this from economies of scale; higher demand creates higher supply. Therefore, the lower the demand, the lower the supply. This might be an over-simplification of this dynamic - yet how lovely it is to imagine all slaughterhouses and factory farms shutting down because the demand for meat and dairy was not enough to sustain their operations. If you enjoy using your imagination to create the world that you want to be a part of, then I suggest you join my cosmickittyinspace/Ana Not Ana Discord Channel where we do exactly that.

This distinction exists because it’s more important to understand the decision than to use a word that can sometimes be polarizing and triggering. The goal of this guidebook is to make it easier for more people to make the switch to veganism and/or a plant-based lifestyle; not to separate or shame anyone away. This is not about triggering people. People are triggered enough (especially with the current state of the world) - this is about providing such an irresistible alternative that is not only more affordable and accessible over time, but also makes you feel better.

I AM NOT VEGAN. I am plant-based. This means that if I’m in Italy and visit a farmer on a no-kill farm, I will 100% eat their mozzarella and gelato made from their cow's milk and have fresh eggs from their chickens. After living and working on different farms for 10 months in the South before returning to New York, I realized that it’s not about “not eating eggs” or “never eating cheese ever again.” It’s more about UNDERSTANDING WHY I have chosen to avoid the products that come from the egg and dairy industry as it currently stands.
I’ve been on this journey for over 7 years; I’ve realized that it’s more about not giving my PURCHASING POWER to the factory farm industry than it is about being militant toward my dietary decisions.

This is the part where I teach you how to replace your current pantry/fridge items to make this process THAT MUCH EASIER. Here are some recipes we'll cover. I've included affiliate links in the main text to make the transition even easier if you don’t cook, don't have access to a kitchen, or prefer buying these products instead of making them. Again, this guidebook is focused on making things easier for you, not harder. Simply hover over the item at the top of the page eg: MILK BUTTER CHEESE and a link will take you to my Amazon affiliate page. This is how I keep this sustainable while providing free material.
Please email cosmickittyinspace@gmail.com with any questions about this.
Okay, now that that’s all out of the way, let’s go make your fridge and pantry cruelty-free!
THE FUN PART

variants.name: Oat Milk (Easiest)
steps: Strain through a nut milk bag or fine towel.
variants.tips: Tip: Don't overblend or use warm water, or it can become slimy.

variants.name: Cashew Milk (No Straining Needed)
ingredients: 1 cup raw cashews (soaked 2–4 hours or overnight)
steps: Blend for 1–2 minutes until completely smooth.
Because cashews blend so finely, you often don't need to strain them.

variants.name: Coconut Milk
steps: Great for curries, smoothies, and desserts.

variants.name: Sunflower Seed Milk
variants.tips: A great nut-free option.

variants.name: Soy Milk (Highest Protein)
steps: Boil gently for about 20 minutes, stirring often.
variants.tips: Soy milk takes a little more work because it needs to be cooked after blending. Soy milk is naturally high in protein and works well in cooking and baking.

variants.name: Homemade Vegan Butter
ingredients: ½ cup neutral oil (such as sunflower or avocado)
steps: Blend until emulsified, pour into a container, and chill until firm.

variants.name: Cashew "Cheese"
ingredients: Enough water for a creamy consistency
variants.tips: Use it as a dip, pasta sauce, or sandwich spread.

variants.name: Classic Cashew Vegan Cream Cheese
ingredients: 1 teaspoon white miso (optional, adds cheesy tang)
1–2 tablespoons plant yogurt or sauerkraut brine (optional, for a cultured flavor)
steps: Blend everything until completely smooth and creamy.
variants.tips: Keeps about 5–7 days in the fridge.

variants.name: Nut-Free Sunflower Seed Cream Cheese
steps: Soak seeds 4 hours; blend until smooth.
variants.tips: This is cheaper, allergy-friendly, and great for feeding groups.

variants.name: High-Protein Tofu Cream Cheese
variants.tips: This is probably the easiest everyday version and has more protein than cashew cream cheese.

variants.name: Easy High-Protein Vegan Cottage Cheese (Tofu Version)
ingredients: ½ cup unsweetened vegan yogurt (soy works best)
1 tablespoon tahini or cashew butter (optional, adds richness)
steps: Drain tofu and gently crumble it with your hands into small curds.
In a separate bowl, whisk yogurt, lemon juice, vinegar, nutritional yeast, salt, and tahini.
Fold the tofu crumbles into the creamy mixture.
Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes so the flavors blend.
variants.tips: Texture tip: Don’t mash the tofu too much—you want little "curds" like traditional cottage cheese. **For a fermented "real cream cheese" flavor, you can let the cashew version sit with a probiotic capsule or a spoonful of live vegan yogurt for 12–24 hours before refrigerating. It develops that tangy cultured taste similar to traditional cream cheese.

variants.name: Nut-Free, Soy-Free Version (Seed-Based)
ingredients: ½ cup mashed white beans or crumbled tofu alternative (for curd texture)
steps: Blend the creamy part, then mix with the chunky part.

variants.name: Protein Boost
steps: Pair with legumes or whole grains
variants.tips: If you're aiming for a whole-food vegan "athlete" version:

ingredients: 2 cups (480 ml) unsweetened soy milk (the kind made from just soybeans and water works best)
1 tablespoon plain vegan yogurt with live active cultures (or 1–2 probiotic capsules containing live cultures)
1 tablespoon tapioca starch or cornstarch (optional, for a thicker yogurt)
1 teaspoon maple syrup or sugar (optional, helps feed the cultures)
steps: Pour the soy milk into a saucepan.
Whisk in the starch if using.
Stir a few tablespoons of the cooled milk into the vegan yogurt until smooth.
Mix it back into the pot.
Transfer to a clean glass jar.
Refrigerate for at least 6 hours before eating.

content.title: Yogurt
content.intro: It will continue to thicken as it chills.

variants.name: For an Extra Thick "Greek-Style" Yogurt
steps: After chilling, line a strainer with cheesecloth or a nut milk bag and let the yogurt drain in the refrigerator for 2–6 hours. The longer it drains, the thicker it becomes.

variants.name: Best Milk Choices
ingredients: Soy milk – highest protein, thickest and most reliable.
Coconut milk – rich and creamy but lower in protein.
Oat or almond milk – can work but usually need additional thickeners for a creamy texture.

variants.name: Storage
steps: Keeps in the refrigerator for 5–7 days.
Save 2 tablespoons from each batch to use as the starter for your next batch.

content.title: Sour Cream
content.intro: Vegan sour cream is one of the easiest dairy alternatives to make because the main goal is creaminess + tang. Here are a few versions depending on what you have.

variants.name: Classic Cashew Sour Cream (Closest to Dairy)
ingredients: 1 tablespoon unsweetened vegan yogurt (optional, for extra tang)
steps: Blend everything until completely smooth and silky.
variants.tips: Flavor adjustment: More lemon = brighter. More vinegar = sharper sour cream flavor. More salt = more "dairy-like".

variants.name: Nut-Free Sunflower Sour Cream
variants.tips: Great for allergy-friendly cooking classes.

variants.name: High-Protein Tofu Sour Cream (Fastest)
variants.tips: This is great for: tacos, baked potatoes, chili, vegan stroganoff, dips

variants.name: Cultured Coconut Sour Cream (Most Traditional Flavor)
variants.tips: (The coconut flavor can be reduced by adding more tang and herbs.)

variants.name: Classic Vegan Mayo (Aquafaba Version)
ingredients: ¼ cup aquafaba (liquid from a can of chickpeas)
1 cup neutral oil (avocado, sunflower, grapeseed, or canola)
steps: Add aquafaba, lemon juice, vinegar, mustard, and salt to a tall jar.
Use an immersion blender and blend for 10–15 seconds.
Slowly drizzle in oil while blending.
Keep blending until thick and creamy.
Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to firm up.
variants.tips: (Closest to traditional mayo) Keeps about 1 week in the fridge.

variants.name: Whole-Food Vegan Mayo (No Refined Oil)
variants.tips: This is more like a cashew aioli/spread and works beautifully in: sandwiches, wraps, potato salad, coleslaw, vegan tuna salad.

variants.name: Flavor upgrades
ingredients: Chipotle mayo: add smoked paprika + chipotle
Ranch mayo: add dill, parsley, garlic, onion powder
Lemon herb mayo: add fresh herbs + extra lemon

content.title: Tzatziki
content.intro: Vegan tzatziki is one of the easiest dairy-free sauces to make. It’s basically a creamy cucumber-herb sauce with yogurt, garlic, lemon, and dill.

variants.name: Classic Vegan Tzatziki
ingredients: 1 cup unsweetened vegan yogurt (soy works best for protein; coconut works for richness)
steps: Squeeze out as much water as possible using a clean towel (this prevents watery tzatziki).
Mix yogurt, cucumber, garlic, lemon, olive oil, herbs, salt, and pepper.
Let sit in the fridge for 30 minutes–2 hours so the flavors develop.

content.title: Ranch
content.intro: Vegan Ranch is actually very easy to make. The secret is creating the creamy base + tang + herbs + garlic/onion flavor that dairy ranch gets from buttermilk and seasonings.

variants.name: Classic Vegan Ranch Dressing
ingredients: 1 cup unsweetened vegan yogurt (soy yogurt works great)
¼ cup vegan mayo (optional, makes it richer)
1 teaspoon garlic powder (or 1 fresh garlic clove)
steps: Let sit in the fridge for 30 minutes so the herbs bloom.

content.title: Caesar Dressing
content.intro: Vegan Caesar dressing is one of the best dairy-free sauces because the “Caesar” flavor comes less from dairy and more from umami + garlic + lemon + creaminess. The traditional anchovy flavor can be recreated with capers, miso, or seaweed.

variants.name: Vegan Caesar Dressing (Cashew-Based)
ingredients: 1 cup raw cashews (soaked 4–6 hours or boiled 15–20 minutes)
1 tablespoon white miso (optional but adds amazing umami)

variants.name: Extra “Restaurant-Style” Caesar Flavor
ingredients: ½ teaspoon dulse flakes or crushed nori (for ocean umami)
Roasted garlic instead of raw garlic

content.title: Aioli
content.intro: A vegan aioli alternative is basically a creamy garlic sauce. Traditional aioli is an emulsion of garlic + oil (often with egg in modern versions), so the vegan versions recreate the richness with nuts, seeds, tofu, or beans.

variants.name: Classic Vegan Garlic Aioli (Cashew)
ingredients: 1 cup raw cashews (soaked 4–6 hours or boiled 15–20 minutes)

variants.name: Flavor variations
ingredients: Spicy aioli: smoked paprika + chili flakes
Lemon pepper aioli: extra lemon zest + cracked pepper
Olive aioli: blend in chopped olives or capers
Roasted garlic aioli: roast garlic first for a sweeter flavor

variants.tips: For a whole-food vegan “mother sauce” collection, aioli is a great base because you can turn the same creamy mixture into ranch, Caesar, chipotle sauce, garlic spread, or sandwich mayo just by changing the seasonings.

variants.name: Easy Vegan Ricotta
ingredients: 1½ cups raw cashews, soaked 2–4 hours and drained
½ cup firm or extra-firm tofu, pressed
1 tbsp olive oil (optional, for extra richness)
steps: Add everything except the water to a food processor.
Pulse several times rather than blending continuously. You want crumbly, ricotta-like curds, not a completely smooth paste.
Add water 1 tablespoon at a time until it reaches your preferred consistency.
Refrigerate for 30–60 minutes before using. It firms up beautifully.

variants.name: Hollandaise
ingredients: ½ cup raw cashews, soaked 2–4 hours and drained
½ tsp turmeric — mostly for that gorgeous yellow color
steps: Blend: Add everything to a high-speed blender.
Blend until silky smooth, adding water 1 tbsp at a time if it's too thick.
Warm: Pour into a small saucepan and heat over low heat, whisking constantly for 2–4 minutes.
Don't let it boil—the sauce can become too thick or separate.
Taste and adjust the lemon, salt, and Dijon until it's bright and tangy.

variants.name: Easy Gravy
ingredients: 2 tbsp vegan butter or olive oil
steps: Make the roux: Melt the vegan butter over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 1–2 minutes, stirring constantly.
Add broth slowly: Gradually whisk in the vegetable broth to avoid lumps.
Season: Add soy sauce, nutritional yeast, onion powder, garlic powder, thyme, and pepper.
Simmer: Cook for 5–8 minutes, whisking occasionally, until thick and glossy.
Taste: Add more soy sauce for depth or salt if needed.

variants.name: Sunflower Seeds (Best All-Around Cashew Replacement)
ingredients: High in vitamin E, magnesium, and healthy fats
steps: 1 cup cashews → 1 cup soaked sunflower seeds
variants.tips: Best for: cream cheese, sour cream, ranch, cheese sauces, aioli. Tip: Soak 4–6 hours or boil 15 minutes.

variants.name: White Beans (Budget + High Protein)
variants.tips: Best for: creamy sauces, dips, Alfredo, hummus-style spreads. Creates a surprisingly creamy texture.

variants.name: Silken Tofu (Highest Protein)
variants.tips: Best for: sour cream, mayo, ranch, desserts, mousse

variants.name: Macadamia Nuts (Luxury Cashew Substitute)
variants.tips: Best for: cheesecake, cream sauces, fancy desserts. Cons: Usually more expensive.

variants.name: Hemp Hearts
variants.tips: Best for: sauces, dressings, smoothies

variants.name: Coconut (Creamiest but Has Flavor)
variants.tips: Best for: curries, desserts, whipped creams. Not ideal when you want a neutral “cheese” flavor.

content.heading: BUT WHAT ABOUT VITAMIN B12?
paragraphs: The myth that you can “only get B12 from animal products” must be debunked. B12 actually comes from microbes, not animals!

Animals don't magically create B12. Certain microorganisms make it. Animals acquire B12 through their food and microbial communities, while humans can get it directly from B12-producing microorganisms through fortified foods and supplements.
So where does B12 come from?

Vitamin B12 is made by certain microorganisms—mainly bacteria and archaea. Plants and animals don't manufacture B12 themselves. Historically, animals get B12 by consuming microorganisms or foods contaminated with B12-producing microbes, and then B12 accumulates in their tissues. In modern food systems, animals also commonly receive B12 supplements, so the B12 found in meat, milk, and eggs ultimately comes from microbial production anyway.

content.heading: Why don't plants have B12?
paragraphs: Plants generally don't need B12 for their own biology, so they don't produce or store it. That's why ordinary fruits, vegetables, grains, beans, nuts, and seeds aren't reliable B12 sources.
Some algae and fermented foods can contain B12 or B12-like compounds, but their amounts and forms can be inconsistent.
The fascinating vegan takeaway
B12 isn't really an “animal vitamin.” It's a microbial vitamin. That's why vegans can get B12 from fortified plant foods or B12 supplements without needing animals as the middleman.
Adults need about 2.4 mcg of vitamin B12 per day. Pregnant people need 2.6 mcg, and breastfeeding people need 2.8 mcg.
mcg stands for microgram (also written µg). It’s a very small unit of weight: 1 microgram (mcg) = 1/1,000,000 of a gram. 1,000 mcg = 1 milligram (mg).
So 2.4 mcg of B12 is a tiny amount — but B12 is a vitamin the body needs in very small quantities.
